prompt: When a colleague says "let's circle back", they want to…
funFact: "Circle back" consistently tops surveys of most-hated office jargon.

prompt: What does "OOO" mean in an auto-reply?
funFact: The triple-O auto-reply dates back to Microsoft Exchange in the 1990s.

prompt: A "standup" meeting is supposed to be…
funFact: Standing is the whole mechanism: the discomfort is meant to be the timer.

prompt: What does "ASAP" stand for?
funFact: It spread through military signal traffic, where every extra character cost transmission time.

prompt: "Touch base" means to…
funFact: It comes from baseball, where touching the base is the one thing you must not forget to do.

prompt: A meeting invite marked "FYI only" is asking you to…
funFact: FYI predates email by decades — it was office-memo shorthand long before anyone had an inbox.

prompt: What does "CC" do on an email?
funFact: It stands for carbon copy — the flimsy second sheet a typist put behind the original.

prompt: What does "HR" stand for in a company?
funFact: The phrase was coined by an economist in 1893, but no company had a department for it until much later.

prompt: "Bandwidth", in office talk, means…
funFact: Borrowing it from engineering lets people decline work without ever saying the word no.

prompt: What does "WFH" mean?
funFact: The abbreviation existed for years as a rare perk before it briefly became the default.

prompt: What does "EOD" usually mean in work chat?
funFact: Pro tip: whose timezone is "end of day"? Nobody has ever agreed.

prompt: "Low-hanging fruit" refers to…
funFact: Orchard workers actually pick low fruit last — it bruises less in the basket.

prompt: "Boiling the ocean" describes a plan that is…
funFact: Consultants use it as a warning; the phrase is often traced to Mark Twain as a joke about ambition.

prompt: On an email, "BCC" hides a recipient from…
funFact: Replying all to a message you were blind-copied on is the classic way to reveal yourself.

prompt: "Blue sky thinking" asks a team to…
funFact: The instruction is usually followed within minutes by someone naming the budget.

prompt: A project "post-mortem" exists to do what?
funFact: Some firms run a "pre-mortem" instead — imagining the failure first, before anything has gone wrong.

prompt: "Take it offline" in a meeting means…
funFact: The phrase survived the move to video calls, where absolutely nothing is offline.

prompt: What does signing an "NDA" stop you doing?
funFact: The document that stops you working elsewhere is a different one entirely — a non-compete.

prompt: A "dotted line" report means you also answer to…
funFact: The name is literal: on the org chart the second relationship is drawn as a dashed line.

prompt: "Scope creep" describes a project that…
funFact: It rarely arrives as one big change; it arrives as a series of small reasonable ones.

prompt: What does KPI stand for?
funFact: The concept traces back to 1950s French "tableau de bord" management dashboards.

prompt: Which company popularized "20% time" for side projects?
funFact: Gmail and AdSense both started as 20% projects.

prompt: Which country gave us "karoshi", meaning death from overwork?
funFact: The word entered official use in the 1980s, when the deaths began appearing in labour statistics.

prompt: The Peter Principle says people are promoted until they…
funFact: It was published as satire in 1969, then studied seriously and found to hold up rather well.

prompt: Which management approach is Toyota famous for pioneering?
funFact: Any worker on the line could halt the whole factory by pulling a cord — that was the point.

prompt: Parkinson's Law says work expands to fill…
funFact: It appeared in a 1955 magazine essay about the civil service, and was meant as mockery.

prompt: The phrase "think outside the box" comes from…
funFact: The puzzle is solved by drawing past the square the dots imply — a box nobody actually drew.

prompt: A Gantt chart plots tasks against what?
funFact: Henry Gantt drew his by hand in 1910; every bar had to be redrawn when a date moved.

prompt: What did the word "deadline" originally describe?
funFact: Prisoners who crossed the line at a Civil War camp were shot, which is a firmer deadline than most.

prompt: Brainstorming was popularised by someone working in…
funFact: Alex Osborn set out the rules in 1953; studies since suggest people generate more ideas alone.

prompt: The QWERTY layout was originally designed partly to…
funFact: It spaced out common letter pairs so mechanical arms wouldn't collide.

prompt: In which decade did the first office cubicle debut?
funFact: Designer Robert Propst called later cramped versions "monolithic insanity" and regretted the invention.

prompt: Which company was founded to sell playing cards?
funFact: It also ran taxis and a chain of love hotels before deciding that toys were the better business.

prompt: The Post-it note began as a failed attempt to make…
funFact: The weak adhesive sat unused for years until a colleague wanted a bookmark that would stay put.

prompt: Which company began as a grocery trader selling dried fish and noodles?
funFact: The name means "three stars", chosen to suggest something big and everlasting.

prompt: The "elevator pitch" takes its name from…
options: The length of a lift ride
funFact: The premise is that you have caught the one person you needed, and roughly thirty seconds of them.

prompt: Which company sold the first commercial photocopier?
funFact: Market research advised against it: nobody could see why an office would need copies of anything.

prompt: What did Berkshire Hathaway originally manufacture?
funFact: Warren Buffett has called buying the failing mill the worst investment decision he ever made.

prompt: Which company's chief executive wrote "Only the Paranoid Survive"?
funFact: Andy Grove had already bet the company once, abandoning memory chips for processors.

prompt: Which car maker started out building weaving looms?
funFact: The loom business was sold to fund the first cars, and the family changed a letter of its name.
